title: Sew up a torn seam
safetyTips: Keep fingers clear of the needle point.
Work in good light and take breaks to avoid eye strain.

steps.title: Turn the item inside out
steps.detail: This hides the stitches on the finished side.

steps.title: Pin the seam
steps.detail: Line up both edges along the old seam line and pin so the fabric stays put.

steps.title: Thread and knot
steps.detail: Thread the needle, double the thread, and tie a knot at the end.

steps.title: Sew small backstitches
steps.detail: Start about half an inch before the opening and sew small, even backstitches along the old seam line. Backstitches are the strongest hand stitch.

steps.title: Knot and trim
steps.detail: Finish half an inch past the opening, tie off the thread, and trim the extra.

stopIf: The fabric around the tear is thin or shredded — a patch or a tailor will hold better.

title: Free a stuck zipper
safetyTips: Pull gently — forcing a zipper can tear the fabric or break teeth.

steps.title: Find what's stuck
steps.detail: Look for fabric caught in the slider, or teeth that are bent or missing.

steps.title: Free caught fabric
steps.detail: Pull the fabric away from the slider while you ease the slider backward, a little at a time.

steps.title: Lubricate the teeth
steps.detail: Rub a graphite pencil or bar soap along the teeth on both sides.

steps.title: Work the slider
steps.detail: Slide it up and down slowly until it moves freely.

steps.title: Tighten a loose slider
steps.detail: If the zipper closes and then splits open, gently squeeze the back of the slider with pliers — a tiny bit on each side — and test again.

stopIf: Teeth are missing or the slider is cracked — a tailor can replace the zipper or slider.

title: Sew on a missing button
safetyTips: Keep fingers clear of the needle point.
Work in bright light so the stitches stay neat.

steps.title: Mark the spot
steps.detail: Line the button up with its buttonhole and mark where the old thread was.

steps.title: Thread and knot
steps.detail: Thread the needle, double the thread, and tie a small knot at the end.

steps.title: Leave a little space
steps.detail: Lay a toothpick across the button so the stitches aren't too tight to button easily.

steps.title: Sew through the holes
steps.detail: Pass the needle up and down through the holes about six times until the button feels secure.

steps.title: Wrap the shank
steps.detail: Remove the toothpick, bring the needle up under the button, and wind the thread around the stitches a few times.

steps.title: Tie off and trim
steps.detail: Push the needle to the back, knot it, and trim the extra thread.

title: Patch a hole in jeans
safetyTips: Stand the iron on its heel when you're not using it, and unplug it when you're done.
Keep fingers clear of the needle point.

steps.title: Trim loose threads
steps.detail: Snip long, loose threads around the hole so the edges lie flat. Don't make the hole bigger.

steps.title: Cut the patch
steps.detail: Cut a patch at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) bigger than the hole on every side. Round the corners so they don't peel up.

steps.title: Place it inside the leg
steps.detail: Turn the jeans inside out and slide cardboard into the leg so you only work on one layer. Lay the patch over the hole — glue side down for iron-on.

steps.title: Attach the patch
steps.detail: Iron-on: press with a hot, dry iron for the time on the package, usually 30-60 seconds. Sew-on: pin it and stitch around the edge with small stitches.

steps.title: Reinforce the hole
steps.detail: From the outside, sew small back-and-forth stitches across the hole to hold the frayed edges down. This keeps it from wearing through again.

steps.title: Let it cool and wash
steps.detail: Let an iron-on patch cool completely before bending it. Wash the jeans inside out to help it last.

title: Fix a fallen hem
safetyTips: Keep fingers clear of the needle point.
If you use an iron, keep it moving and unplug it when you're done.

steps.title: Fold along the old crease
steps.detail: Fold the hem back along its original crease and pin every few inches. Pressing it with an iron makes the fold crisp.

steps.title: Thread the needle
steps.detail: Use a single strand about 18 inches (45 cm) long and knot the end.

steps.title: Overlap the old stitches
steps.detail: Start about an inch before the loose section so the new stitches lock the old ones in place.

steps.title: Slip stitch
steps.detail: Catch one or two threads of the outer fabric, then slide the needle about 1/4 inch (6 mm) along inside the fold. Tiny catches stay invisible from the outside.

steps.title: Knot and press
steps.detail: Finish an inch past the loose section, tie off inside the hem, and trim. No-sew option: put fusible hem tape inside the fold and press following the package.

title: Darn a small hole in a sweater or sock
tools: Yarn or thread close to the original
Darning egg or a tennis ball
safetyTips: Use a tennis ball or darning egg inside — never a glass object like a light bulb, which can break.
A blunt needle slides between knit stitches instead of splitting them.

steps.title: Support the hole
steps.detail: Slip the darning egg or ball inside so the fabric is smooth but not stretched.

steps.title: Outline a frame
steps.detail: Sew small running stitches in a square about 1/2 inch (1 cm) outside the hole, into solid fabric.

steps.title: Lay the long threads
steps.detail: Run yarn back and forth across the hole from one side of the frame to the other, keeping the lines close and parallel.

steps.title: Weave across
steps.detail: Turn 90 degrees and weave over and under the long threads, row by row, until the hole is filled like a tiny basket weave.

steps.title: Hide the tail
steps.detail: Weave the end into the back of the stitches instead of knotting it, so it stays soft and flat.

title: Troubleshoot a lamp that won't turn on
tools: A working outlet to test with
safetyTips: Unplug the lamp before touching the bulb socket.
Use a bulb at or below the maximum wattage printed near the socket.
Don't open the lamp base or attempt any rewiring yourself.

steps.title: Unplug the lamp
steps.detail: Never work on a lamp while it is plugged in.

steps.title: Check the cord
steps.detail: Look along the whole cord and plug. If you see cracks, frayed spots, or melted plastic, stop — the lamp needs a new cord from a pro.

steps.title: Swap the bulb
steps.detail: Try a bulb you know works to rule out a dead bulb. Let a hot bulb cool first.

steps.title: Test the outlet
steps.detail: Plug the lamp into an outlet you know works, like one where a phone charger works.

steps.title: Check the switch
steps.detail: Click the switch a few times. If it feels loose or crunchy, or the lamp flickers when you touch it, take it to a repair cafe or replace the lamp.

stopIf: The cord is cracked, frayed, or melted.
You see scorch marks or smell burning.
The bulb socket is loose, bent, or blackened.

title: Clean a fan that won't spin
tools: Light machine oil (only if the manual says to oil it)
safetyTips: Always unplug the fan before cleaning it.
Don't open the sealed motor housing or touch a damaged cord.

steps.title: Unplug and inspect
steps.detail: Check the cord, plug, and blades for damage before touching anything else.

steps.title: Clear dust buildup
steps.detail: Brush and vacuum the grille, blades, and vents so air can move again. Many box fans have a grille that unclips for cleaning.

steps.title: Free the blades
steps.detail: Turn the blades by hand. Pull out stuck dust, hair, or debris around the center hub.

steps.title: Oil only if allowed
steps.detail: If the manual points out an oil port, add one or two drops of light machine oil. Skip this step if it doesn't.

steps.title: Test the fan
steps.detail: Plug it back in and run it for a minute. If it hums but doesn't turn, or smells hot, unplug it and stop.

stopIf: The motor hums without spinning after cleaning.
You smell burning or see scorch marks.

title: Fix a toaster lever that won't stay down
safetyTips: Unplug the toaster and let it cool before cleaning it.
Never put metal tools or your fingers into the slots.

steps.title: Check the power first
steps.detail: Many toasters use a magnet that only holds the lever down when the toaster has power. Plug it into an outlet you know works and try again.

steps.title: Unplug and cool down
steps.detail: If it still pops up, unplug the toaster and let it cool completely.

steps.title: Empty the crumbs
steps.detail: Slide out the crumb tray and empty it. Then turn the toaster upside down over the sink and gently tap out loose crumbs.

steps.title: Clean around the lever
steps.detail: Brush along the lever slot and the outside of the slots so crumbs don't jam the latch.

steps.title: Test the lever
steps.detail: Plug it back in and press the lever. If it still won't stay down, the latch inside has failed — recycle the toaster rather than opening it.

title: Restore a vacuum's suction
safetyTips: Unplug the vacuum (or remove the battery) before you open anything.
Point scissors away from your hand when you cut hair off the brush roll.

steps.title: Unplug and empty it
steps.detail: Empty the bin or change the bag. Many vacuums lose suction when the bag or bin is more than two-thirds full.

steps.title: Clean the filters
steps.detail: Tap dust off the filters over a trash can. Rinse only filters the manual calls washable, and let them dry for a full 24 hours before putting them back.

steps.title: Clear the hose
steps.detail: Detach the hose and look through it toward a light. Push out clogs gently with a broom handle.

steps.title: Free the brush roll
steps.detail: Flip the vacuum over, cut away wrapped hair and string, and check that the belt isn't broken or slipping.

steps.title: Test it
steps.detail: Put it back together, plug it in, and feel the suction at the hose.

stopIf: It smells hot or like burning rubber.
The cord is damaged.
The motor sounds like it's grinding.

title: Descale a slow coffee maker
tools: White vinegar or a descaling solution
safetyTips: Check your manual first — some brands require their own descaling solution.
Let the hot vinegar water cool before you pour it out.
Don't open the base or the heating plate.

steps.title: Empty and rinse
steps.detail: Throw out old grounds and rinse the carafe and filter basket.

steps.title: Fill with the descaling mix
steps.detail: Fill the water tank with equal parts white vinegar and water, or follow the descaler's directions.

steps.title: Run half a cycle, then pause
steps.detail: Start a brew cycle, turn it off halfway, and let it sit for 30 minutes so the mix can dissolve mineral buildup.

steps.title: Finish and flush
steps.detail: Finish the cycle, then run 2-3 full cycles of plain water to rinse out the vinegar taste.

steps.title: Repeat if needed
steps.detail: If it still brews slowly, descale one more time.

stopIf: Water leaks from the base.
It trips the breaker or smells like burning.

title: Tighten wobbly furniture
safetyTips: Ask for a second set of hands when flipping heavy furniture.
Don't overtighten screws in particleboard — they strip easily.

steps.title: Find the loose joint
steps.detail: Rock the furniture gently and watch which joint moves or squeaks.

steps.title: Tighten the hardware
steps.detail: Snug up every screw and bolt you can find, including corner brackets under the seat or frame.

steps.title: Re-glue wooden joints
steps.detail: For a loose wooden joint, work a little wood glue into the gap and press it together. Wipe away squeeze-out with a damp rag.

steps.title: Clamp and dry
steps.detail: Clamp or strap the joint and let the glue dry for the time on the bottle — usually overnight — before anyone uses it.

stopIf: A leg, rail, or frame piece is cracked — that's a structural repair.

title: Fix a sticking drawer
tools: Candle, paraffin wax, or bar soap (wood runners)
safetyTips: Empty heavy drawers before you take them out.
Tall dressers can tip over when drawers are pulled out — anchor them to the wall.
Use silicone spray in a ventilated room and keep it off fabric.

steps.title: Empty and remove the drawer
steps.detail: Take everything out, then lift or release the drawer from its slides. Many metal slides have a small release lever on each side.

steps.title: Find the cause
steps.detail: Look for loose screws, a bent slide, debris in the track, or shiny worn spots where wood is rubbing.

steps.title: Clean the tracks
steps.detail: Wipe dust and crumbs out of the runners and the cabinet opening.

steps.title: Tighten the hardware
steps.detail: Snug any loose slide or drawer-front screws without overtightening.

steps.title: Lubricate
steps.detail: Rub wax or bar soap on wooden runners, or mist silicone spray on metal slides. Slide the drawer in and out a few times to spread it.

title: Adjust a sagging cabinet door
tools: Wooden toothpicks and wood glue (for stripped holes)
safetyTips: Support the door with one hand while you loosen screws so it doesn't drop.
Glass cabinet doors are heavy and fragile — get a helper.

steps.title: Find the problem hinge
steps.detail: Open and close the door slowly, watching which hinge moves or which corner rubs.

steps.title: Tighten the mounting screws
steps.detail: Tighten the screws holding the hinge to the cabinet and to the door.

steps.title: Fix stripped holes
steps.detail: If a screw just spins, take it out, push glue-dipped toothpicks into the hole, snap them off flush, let the glue dry, then drive the screw back in.

steps.title: Use the adjustment screws
steps.detail: Hidden (European) hinges have adjustment screws: one moves the door side to side, another moves it in and out. Turn a quarter turn at a time.

steps.title: Check the gaps
steps.detail: Aim for even gaps around the door and a door that closes without rubbing.

title: Replace an office chair wheel
tools: Replacement casters with the same stem size
safetyTips: Lay the chair upside down on a rug or towel, not on its back on a hard floor.
Don't try to remove or repair the gas cylinder in the center — it's pressurized.

steps.title: Flip the chair
steps.detail: Turn the chair upside down on a soft surface.

steps.title: Pull out the old wheel
steps.detail: Grip the wheel and pull firmly straight out. If it's stuck, pry gently between the wheel and the base with a flathead screwdriver.

steps.title: Match the stem
steps.detail: Take the old wheel to the store or measure its stem. Most office chairs use a 7/16 inch (11 mm) grip-ring stem.

steps.title: Push in the new wheel
steps.detail: Press the new stem into the hole until it snaps in. Tap it with a rubber mallet if needed.

steps.title: Test it
steps.detail: Turn the chair upright and roll it around before sitting down.

stopIf: The base is cracked — replace the base, and don't sit on the chair until you do.

title: Patch a flat bike tube
tools: Bucket of water (to find the hole)
safetyTips: Let all the air out before taking the tire off.
Use plastic tire levers, not screwdrivers — metal can puncture the tube.
Check that the wheel is tight and the brakes work before you ride.

steps.title: Let out the air
steps.detail: Let out any air that's left. For rim brakes, open the brake's quick release so the wheel can come out.

steps.title: Remove the wheel and tube
steps.detail: Take off the wheel, use tire levers to pry one side of the tire off the rim, and pull out the tube.

steps.title: Find the hole
steps.detail: Pump a little air into the tube and listen, or dip it in water and watch for bubbles. Mark the spot.

steps.title: Find what caused it
steps.detail: Carefully run your fingers around the inside of the tire to find glass, thorns, or wire. Remove it, or the new patch will puncture too.

steps.title: Apply the patch
steps.detail: Roughen the area with the kit's sandpaper, spread a thin layer of glue, wait until it looks dry, then press the patch on firmly.

steps.title: Reinstall and inflate
steps.detail: Tuck the tube in, seat the tire by hand, and pump to the pressure printed on the tire's sidewall. Close the brake quick release before you ride.

title: Lube a dry bike chain
safetyTips: Keep fingers away from the chainrings while you turn the pedals.
Keep lube off the rims and brake pads — it makes brakes slip.

steps.title: Wipe the chain
steps.detail: Hold a rag around the chain and backpedal to wipe off dirt and old grease.

steps.title: Apply lube
steps.detail: Add one drop to each roller while slowly backpedaling.

steps.title: Spin and wipe
steps.detail: Turn the pedals for a minute, then wipe away the extra. Lube belongs inside the chain, not on the outside.

steps.title: Test the ride
steps.detail: Shift through a few gears and listen for squeaks.

title: Adjust a loose or wrong-height bike seat
tools: Hex keys (usually 4, 5, or 6 mm) or a wrench
safetyTips: Never raise the seat post above the minimum-insertion line marked on the post.
Tighten bolts firmly but don't overtighten, especially carbon parts — use a torque wrench if the part lists a torque.

steps.title: Loosen the clamp
steps.detail: Open the quick-release lever or loosen the bolt where the seat post enters the frame.

steps.title: Set the height
steps.detail: With your heel on the pedal at its lowest point, your leg should be almost straight. Pedaling with the ball of your foot then leaves a slight bend in the knee.

steps.title: Line it up
steps.detail: Point the nose of the seat straight along the top tube.

steps.title: Tighten the clamp
steps.detail: Close the quick release firmly or tighten the bolt until the seat won't twist when you push on it.

steps.title: Level the seat
steps.detail: If the seat tilts, loosen the bolt under it, set it level, and retighten.

steps.title: Test ride
steps.detail: Ride slowly somewhere safe and make sure nothing slips.

stopIf: The seat post or frame is cracked.
The clamp won't hold no matter how you tighten it.

title: Adjust rim brake pads
safetyTips: Test the brakes at walking speed before any real ride.
This guide is for rim brakes. Hydraulic or disc brakes go to a bike shop.
Never ride a bike whose brakes don't reliably stop it.

steps.title: Check pad wear
steps.detail: Replace pads if the grooves are worn smooth or the metal holder is close to the rim.

steps.title: Clean the rims
steps.detail: Wipe the braking surface of the rims with a clean rag to remove grime.

steps.title: Align the pads
steps.detail: Loosen the pad bolt and set each pad to hit the middle of the rim's braking surface — never the tire. Retighten firmly.

steps.title: Set the spacing
steps.detail: Turn the barrel adjuster at the brake lever so the pads sit close to the rim but don't rub when the lever is released.

steps.title: Test carefully
steps.detail: Squeeze the lever hard — it should stop well before touching the handlebar. Then walk the bike and brake to confirm it stops.

stopIf: The brakes are hydraulic (fluid-filled hoses).
The brake cable is frayed, or the lever reaches the handlebar.
The rim is cracked or badly worn.

title: Fine-tune shifting with the barrel adjuster
tools: Bike stand, or a helper to lift the back wheel
safetyTips: Keep fingers away from the chain and gears while turning the pedals.
Only turn the barrel adjuster. Leave the limit screws (marked H and L) alone — wrong settings can drop the chain into the spokes.

steps.title: Lift the back wheel
steps.detail: Hang the bike on a stand or have a helper lift the back so you can turn the pedals.

steps.title: Start in the smallest cog
steps.detail: Shift to the smallest rear cog, then click one gear up while turning the pedals.

steps.title: Find the barrel adjuster
steps.detail: It's the small round knob where the cable enters the rear derailleur or the shifter.

steps.title: Adjust a little at a time
steps.detail: If the chain hesitates to climb to the next bigger cog, turn the adjuster counterclockwise a quarter turn. If it's noisy or jumps too far, turn it clockwise.

steps.title: Check every gear
steps.detail: Shift through all the gears while pedaling, then test-ride slowly.

stopIf: The derailleur or its hanger looks bent.
The chain falls off toward the spokes.
Shifting stays rough after adjusting — the chain or cassette may be worn.

title: Reinforce a frayed charging cable
tools: Electrical tape, or a snap-on cable protector
safetyTips: Only do this for low-voltage cables like USB or headphone cords.
If a wall-power cord has exposed wires, stop using it and replace it.
Replace a cable that gets hot, sparks, or has cut wires inside.

steps.title: Unplug the cable
steps.detail: Disconnect it from both the device and the power adapter.

steps.title: Check the damage
steps.detail: If you can see cut or bare inner wires, recycle the cable instead of patching it.

steps.title: Support the bend point
steps.detail: Wrap electrical tape snugly over the fray and an inch onto the plug, or snap on a cable protector. This stops the cable from bending sharply at the weak spot.

steps.title: Test gently
steps.detail: Reconnect and check that it charges without wiggling. Avoid wrapping it tightly around the charger in the future.

title: Clean a phone's charging port
tools: Soft, dry brush (a clean, unused toothbrush works)
safetyTips: Turn the phone off and unplug it first.
Never use metal objects like pins or paper clips — they can short or bend the contacts.
Don't use liquids, compressed air, or heat in the port.

steps.title: Power off
steps.detail: Turn the phone off and take off the case.

steps.title: Look inside
steps.detail: Shine a light into the port. Lint usually packs in at the very back.

steps.title: Loosen lint gently
steps.detail: Slide the toothpick along the back wall and sides of the port to lift lint out. Don't pry at the contacts in the middle.

steps.title: Brush it out
steps.detail: Sweep the port gently with the soft brush.

steps.title: Test with a good cable
steps.detail: Plug in a cable you know works. The connector should click in firmly.

stopIf: The port is loose, bent, or corroded.
The phone still won't charge with a known-good cable — a repair shop can replace the port.

title: Clean sticky keyboard keys
safetyTips: Shut down and unplug the computer (or unplug the keyboard) first.
Only use a lightly dampened swab — never pour liquid on the keys.
Laptop keys clip on with fragile hinges. Don't pry them off unless the manufacturer shows how.

steps.title: Power off
steps.detail: Shut down and unplug the laptop or keyboard.

steps.title: Shake out crumbs
steps.detail: Turn it upside down and tap it gently. Sweep between the keys with a soft brush.

steps.title: Use short bursts of air
steps.detail: Hold the can upright and spray in short bursts at an angle, moving across the rows of keys.

steps.title: Clean sticky keys
steps.detail: Wipe around the sticky key with a swab lightly dampened with isopropyl alcohol, pressing the key several times as you go.

steps.title: Dry and test
steps.detail: Wait 10 minutes for the alcohol to evaporate before turning it back on.

stopIf: Something sugary was spilled inside — a repair shop should clean it before it corrodes.
Keys stay stuck after cleaning.

title: Clean a crackling headphone jack
safetyTips: Power off the device before cleaning the port.
Stop if the jack is loose, bent, or visibly damaged.

steps.title: Turn the device off
steps.detail: Unplug the headphones and any charger before touching the port.

steps.title: Inspect the jack
steps.detail: Shine a light into the jack and look for lint or dust.

steps.title: Clear the port
steps.detail: Sweep it with a soft brush, or gently lift out lint with a wooden toothpick. Don't force anything in.

steps.title: Rule out the headphones
steps.detail: Test with headphones you know work. If they sound fine, your old headphones are the problem.

stopIf: The crackle stays with known-good headphones — the jack likely needs a repair shop.

title: Silence a squeaky door hinge
tools: Petroleum jelly, white lithium grease, or silicone spray
safetyTips: Close the door and work on one hinge pin at a time, so the door stays supported.
Put a paper towel on the floor to catch drips.

steps.title: Close the door
steps.detail: A closed door keeps the hinges lined up while you work.

steps.title: Tap out the pin
steps.detail: Hold a nail under the top hinge pin and tap upward with the hammer until you can pull the pin out.

steps.title: Clean and grease
steps.detail: Wipe the pin clean, then coat it lightly with petroleum jelly, white lithium grease, or silicone spray.

steps.title: Put it back
steps.detail: Slide the pin back in and tap it down. Swing the door a few times to spread the grease, then repeat for the other hinges one at a time.

steps.title: Wipe off extra
steps.detail: Wipe away any drips so they don't collect dust.

title: Tighten a wobbly doorknob
tools: Small flathead screwdriver or hex key (for hidden screws)
safetyTips: Keep the door propped open while the knob is loose so nobody gets locked in or out.

steps.title: Find the screws
steps.detail: Look on the inside plate (the rose) for two screws. Some knobs hide them under a cover that pops off, or use a tiny set screw on the knob's neck.

steps.title: Tighten evenly
steps.detail: Tighten the screws a little at a time, switching between them, until the knob is firm. Overtightening can make the latch stick.

steps.title: Check the latch
steps.detail: Turn the knob both ways and make sure the latch slides in and out smoothly.

steps.title: Tighten the strike plate
steps.detail: If the door won't stay closed, tighten the screws on the metal plate in the door frame.

title: Clear a slow sink drain
safetyTips: Don't mix drain cleaners, and don't plunge if a chemical cleaner is already in the drain — it can splash.
Wear gloves; drain gunk carries bacteria.
Use hot tap water, not boiling water — boiling water can damage plastic pipes and some sinks.

steps.title: Remove the stopper
steps.detail: Lift or unscrew the stopper. Some bathroom stoppers release from a nut on the drain pipe under the sink.

steps.title: Pull out hair and gunk
steps.detail: Use a plastic drain strip or tweezers to pull out hair and buildup.

steps.title: Plunge
steps.detail: Fill the sink with a few inches of water, cover the overflow hole with a wet rag, and plunge firmly 10-15 times.

steps.title: Flush it
steps.detail: Run hot tap water for a minute. For a mild slowdown, pour in 1/2 cup baking soda, then 1 cup vinegar, wait 15 minutes, and flush with hot tap water.

stopIf: Several drains are slow, or water backs up into another fixture — that's a main line clog for a plumber.
You smell sewage.

title: Unclog a showerhead
safetyTips: Vinegar can dull some finishes like brass or nickel, so keep the soak short for those.
Wipe up spills so the tub floor isn't slippery.

steps.title: Fill a bag with vinegar
steps.detail: Pour enough white vinegar into a plastic bag to cover the face of the showerhead.

steps.title: Tie it on
steps.detail: Slip the bag over the showerhead and secure it with a rubber band so the nozzles sit in the vinegar.

steps.title: Let it soak
steps.detail: Wait 30-60 minutes while the vinegar dissolves mineral buildup.

steps.title: Scrub the nozzles
steps.detail: Take off the bag and scrub the face with an old toothbrush. Rub soft rubber nozzles with a finger to push deposits out.

steps.title: Flush it
steps.detail: Run hot water for a minute to rinse out the loosened buildup.

title: Patch a small hole in drywall
tools: Self-adhesive mesh patch (for holes bigger than a nail hole)
safetyTips: Wear a dust mask when sanding.
Homes built before 1980 may have lead paint or asbestos in the wall — don't sand old walls until they've been tested.

steps.title: Clean up the edges
steps.detail: Brush away loose crumbs and press any frayed paper flat.

steps.title: Cover bigger holes
steps.detail: For holes larger than a nail hole, up to about 4 inches, stick a self-adhesive mesh patch over the hole.

steps.title: Apply spackle
steps.detail: Press a thin layer of spackle into the hole with the putty knife, then scrape it flat, a little wider than the hole.

steps.title: Add a second coat
steps.detail: Let it dry (check the label). If it shrank, add another thin coat.

steps.title: Sand and paint
steps.detail: Sand lightly until smooth, wipe off the dust, then prime and paint to match.

stopIf: The hole is bigger than about 4 inches.
You see wires or pipes inside the wall.
The drywall is wet, soft, or moldy.

title: Touch up a scratched wood finish
tools: Wood touch-up marker or wax stick
safetyTips: Test products on a hidden spot first.
Don't sand through veneer — it's thinner than it looks.

steps.title: Clean the surface
steps.detail: Wipe off dust and grime so the touch-up blends in.

steps.title: Match the color
steps.detail: Pick a marker or wax stick close to the wood tone. When unsure, go a shade lighter.

steps.title: Fill the scratch
steps.detail: Rub the touch-up product into the scratch and smooth it flat.

steps.title: Buff it
steps.detail: Let it set, then buff lightly with a soft cloth.

title: Fix a dripping faucet
safetyTips: Turn off the water supply under the sink before starting.
If the shut-off valve won't close, or the pipes are corroded, call a plumber.

steps.title: Shut off the water
steps.detail: Close the shut-off valves under the sink, then open the faucet to drain the line.

steps.title: Cover the drain
steps.detail: Put a rag in the drain so small screws and parts can't fall in.

steps.title: Take off the handle
steps.detail: Pry off the decorative cap, remove the handle screw, and lift off the handle. Snap a photo of each part as you go.

steps.title: Swap the washer or cartridge
steps.detail: Unscrew the stem or pull out the cartridge, and take it to a hardware store to get an exact match.

steps.title: Reassemble and test
steps.detail: Put everything back in reverse order, turn the water on slowly, and check for drips.

stopIf: Water keeps flowing after the valves are closed.
Parts are corroded or crack when you turn them.

title: Fix a running toilet
safetyTips: Set the tank lid on a towel on the floor — lids are heavy and crack easily.
If the tank or supply line is cracked, shut off the water and call a plumber.

steps.title: Lift off the tank lid
steps.detail: Set it down carefully on a towel.

steps.title: Check the chain
steps.detail: Too much slack can catch under the flapper; too little keeps it from closing. Leave about half an inch of slack.

steps.title: Check the water level
steps.detail: Water should sit about an inch below the top of the overflow tube. If it spills into the tube, adjust the float lower.

steps.title: Test the flapper
steps.detail: Press down gently on the flapper. If the running stops, the flapper is worn and leaking.

steps.title: Replace the flapper
steps.detail: Shut off the water at the valve behind the toilet, flush to empty the tank, unhook the old flapper, and clip on a matching new one.

steps.title: Test it
steps.detail: Turn the water back on, let the tank fill, and flush a few times to check.
